strengths: The combination of adversarially generated training problems, bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets, and learned initializations is well motivated. Training without examples from the eventual test datasets is a useful contribution beyond dataset-specific amortization.

The Hilbert projective loss appropriately handles the scaling ambiguity of Sinkhorn potentials. Proposition 4.3 gives a sound contraction-based bound connecting the bootstrapping residual to potential error for positive kernels.

The reported initialization improvements are substantial across four unseen image datasets. For example, Table 2 reduces the mean iterations needed for 0.01 marginal violation on CIFAR from 47 with standard initialization and 17 with Gaussian initialization to 3.

Five independent training runs, confidence intervals, a generator-versus-noise ablation, and runtime measurements strengthen the empirical evidence. The pseudocode, architecture details, hyperparameters, and linked code help reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central universality claim exceeds the evidence. Theorem 4.1 requires equal input/output dimensions and a Lipschitz constraint, whereas the implemented generator maps 392 latent coordinates to 1,568 outputs and does not enforce that constraint. The authors acknowledge these differences but still conclude that generator expressiveness cannot be a bottleneck. Moreover, full support of a hypothetical generator does not establish accurate prediction on every distribution pair after finite training. The demonstrated result is transfer across the tested datasets.

The closest learned baseline, Amos et al. (2022), is explicitly excluded based on an unsupported assertion that it inherently fails out of distribution. Comparing its dual-objective training under comparable synthetic-data and computational budgets is necessary to establish the advantage of the proposed learning procedure. The noise ablation does not resolve this comparison, and the broad claim of being the first meta neural OT solver conflicts with the paper's own discussion of prior meta OT.

The evaluated scalar is inconsistently defined. Algorithm 1 returns the transport-cost term <C, Gamma>, while Section 5.2 defines the reference value as the minimum regularized objective <C, Gamma> - epsilon H(Gamma). These quantities differ even at convergence. The paper must clarify which quantity generates the reported relative errors and specify how the reference solution is computed; otherwise, the few-percent standalone accuracy claim cannot be confidently interpreted.

The evaluation covers only 28-by-28 image histograms, one squared-Euclidean cost, and epsilon = 0.01. Difficult synthetic distributions within this same problem configuration would better test the claimed coverage. Practical efficiency is also incompletely established: Figure 8 omits the Gaussian baseline, and the batch-500 measurements do not establish negligible prediction overhead for other workloads. These limitations matter for the claimed general usefulness of the solver.

There are repairable mathematical errors in the universality argument. ReLU makes q noninvertible and introduces singular probability mass on boundary faces, so Appendix A cannot discard it without qualification when claiming a density at every nonnegative point. Lipschitz continuity also does not imply differentiability everywhere. Appendix B's batch-normalization argument does not establish the required Lipschitz bound from a Gaussian input prior. These corrections would improve rigor, but would still leave the larger gap between the theorem and the implemented generator.
